candidates.topic: Cleopatra's death — the asp myth debunked
candidates.teaser: Everything you know about Cleopatra's death might be completely wrong — and the truth is even stranger.
candidates.video_title: Cleopatra Didn't Die the Way You Think
candidates.video_description: The story of Cleopatra dying from a snake bite is one of history's most famous tales — but modern scholars seriously doubt it ever happened. The real cause of her death may shock you.
candidates.script: Everyone knows Cleopatra died from the bite of an asp snake — except that probably never happened. The snake story comes almost entirely from Roman propaganda written by her enemies. Here's the problem: a single asp bite is rarely fatal, and smuggling a snake large enough to kill quickly into a heavily guarded room is nearly impossible. Modern toxicologists believe she more likely drank a cocktail of hemlock, opium, and wolfsbane — a painless, controlled death fitting a queen who refused to be paraded through Rome in chains. So the most famous death in history might be completely fictional. What else have we been told wrong?

candidates.topic: Lightning strikes Earth 100 times per second
candidates.teaser: Something extraordinary is happening in Earth's atmosphere right now — and it never, ever stops.
candidates.video_title: Earth Is Being Struck by Lightning Right Now
candidates.video_description: At any given moment, around 2,000 thunderstorms are raging across Earth simultaneously. The planet is struck by lightning roughly 100 times every single second — that's 8 million strikes per day.
candidates.script: Right now, as you watch this, the Earth is being struck by lightning 100 times every single second. That's not a guess — it's a constant. At any moment, roughly 2,000 thunderstorms are raging simultaneously across the planet, firing 8 million bolts of lightning every single day. A single bolt reaches temperatures five times hotter than the surface of the sun — around 30,000 Kelvin — and it happens in less than a millisecond. In your lifetime, the Earth will be struck by lightning over 200 trillion times. And here's the twist — all that lightning is actually what makes life on Earth possible. Can you figure out why?

candidates.teaser: There's a tiny shrimp in the ocean that creates one of the loudest sounds on the planet — and it kills with a snap.
candidates.video_title: This Tiny Shrimp Shoots a Sonic Weapon
candidates.video_description: The pistol shrimp can snap its claw so fast it creates a cavitation bubble that briefly reaches the temperature of the sun's surface and kills prey instantly. It's one of the most powerful weapons in nature.
candidates.script: Meet the pistol shrimp — barely the size of your finger — and one of the most terrifying hunters in the ocean. When it snaps its oversized claw, it moves so fast it creates a cavitation bubble — a tiny collapsing void in the water that generates a shockwave reaching 210 decibels, louder than a gunshot. For a fraction of a millisecond, that bubble heats to around 8,000 degrees Fahrenheit — almost as hot as the surface of the sun. The shockwave stuns or kills prey instantly. This shrimp is so loud that during World War Two, submarines used pistol shrimp colonies to hide from enemy sonar. What else is hiding in the deep ocean?

candidates.teaser: There's a glitch in your brain that makes you see the same thing everywhere right after you learn about it — and it has a name.
candidates.video_title: Your Brain Is Playing a Trick on You Daily
candidates.video_description: The Baader-Meinhof phenomenon — also called the frequency illusion — makes you suddenly notice something everywhere after you first encounter it. It's not coincidence. It's a cognitive bias hard-wired into your brain.
candidates.script: Have you ever learned a new word and then heard it three times the same day? Or bought a car and suddenly saw that model everywhere on the road? That's not a coincidence — it's a documented brain glitch called the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon. Your brain has a filter called the reticular activating system that decides what information is worth noticing. The moment something becomes meaningful to you, your brain flags it as important and suddenly pulls it out of the noise it was always buried in. The thing was always there. You just couldn't see it. Which makes you wonder — what else is your brain hiding from you right now?

candidates.topic: The Dyatlov Pass incident — unsolved mystery
candidates.teaser: Nine experienced hikers died under circumstances so bizarre that investigators officially declared the cause 'an unknown compelling force.'
candidates.video_title: 9 Hikers Died — The Cause Was 'Unknown Force'
candidates.video_description: In 1959, nine experienced Soviet hikers were found dead in the Ural Mountains under deeply strange circumstances — torn from their tent from the inside, scattered in the snow, with internal injuries but no external wounds. The case was classified for decades.
candidates.script: In February 1959, nine expert Soviet hikers set up camp on a mountain in the Urals. That night, they sliced open their tent from the inside and ran barefoot into minus-thirty-degree temperatures. They were found scattered across the snow — some with fractured skulls and broken ribs but zero external wounds, as if they'd been crushed from the inside. One woman was missing her tongue and eyes. Soviet investigators closed the case labeling the cause as 'an unknown compelling force.' The files were classified for decades. Scientists today believe an infrasound wave from the mountain triggered mass panic — but nobody agrees. So what really happened that night?
